title: Maximum Number of Robots Within Budget
description: Brute force to optimized: restarting tracking for every start versus a sliding window combining a monotonic deque (max) with a running sum.

content.title: Maximum Number of Robots Within Budget

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

You have n robots, with chargeTimes[i] and runningCosts[i] for each. Running a CONSECUTIVE group of k robots together costs max(chargeTimes in the group) + k * sum(runningCosts in the group). Return the MAXIMUM number of consecutive robots you can run together without the total cost exceeding budget.

blocks.caption: A sliding window, tracked by a monotonic deque (for the max charge time) plus a running sum (for total running cost), directly evaluates each window's cost

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A CONSECUTIVE group's cost depends on both a MAX (charge time) and a SUM (running cost)","A sliding window, needing FAST access to the window's current max (a monotonic deque) alongside a simple running sum"],["\"Maximum size\" of a valid consecutive group, with a budget constraint","A classic variable-size sliding window: expand while possible, shrink from the left whenever the constraint is violated"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

The cost formula combines two different aggregate quantities over the SAME window: the MAXIMUM charge time (only one robot's charge time matters, whichever is largest) and the SUM of running costs (multiplied by how many robots are in the group, since they all run together for the same duration).

blocks.title: Analogy: Renting a Group of Machines With a Shared Setup Fee Plus Per-Machine Running Costs
blocks.text: Imagine renting a consecutive group of machines for a job: there is ONE shared setup fee (determined by whichever machine in the group has the LONGEST setup time, since everyone must wait for it), plus each machine's own running cost, all multiplied by how many machines are running together (since they all run for the same duration). Finding the LARGEST group that still fits within a budget requires tracking both the group's current maximum setup time AND its total running cost as the group's membership changes.

blocks.caption: The window's cost (max charge + k times running sum) is checked after every expansion; exceeding budget triggers shrinking from the left

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: chargeTimes = [3,6,1,3,4], runningCosts = [2,1,3,4,5], budget = 25

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: 3, the largest valid consecutive group size found
5. How Should We Think?

Before recomputing the max charge time and sum of running costs from scratch for every candidate window (expensive), notice that a sliding window, combined with a monotonic deque (for the max) and a running sum, can maintain BOTH quantities incrementally as the window expands and shrinks.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The window's cost formula needs TWO different aggregates: the MAXIMUM charge time (best tracked with a monotonic decreasing deque, exactly as in Sliding Window Maximum) and the SUM of running costs (best tracked with a simple running total, adjusted by addition/subtraction as the window changes).

Observation 2: As the window expands (right pointer moves), the new robot's charge time updates the monotonic deque (popping any now-dominated smaller charge times from the back), and its running cost is simply added to the running sum.

Observation 3: After each expansion, the current window's cost (deque's front + k * running sum) is checked; if it exceeds budget, the window must shrink from the LEFT, removing the leftmost robot's running cost from the sum, and popping it from the deque's FRONT if it happened to be the current max.

Observation 4: The best (largest) window size found throughout this single pass is the final answer, since the window is always exactly as large as currently possible at every point.

This is a variable-size sliding window technique, combining a monotonic deque (for the window's max charge time) with a running sum (for total running cost), shrinking from the left whenever the combined cost exceeds the budget.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each possible starting index, extend the window rightward one robot at a time, tracking the running max charge time and sum of running costs, stopping the moment the cost exceeds budget.
Step by step algorithm

items: For each starting index i, extend the window (index j from i onward), updating the running max charge time and sum of running costs.
At each step, compute the current window's cost; if within budget, update the best size found; if not, stop extending from this starting point (any longer window would only cost more).

codes.python:
def maximum_robots(charge_times, running_costs, budget):
    n = len(charge_times)
    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        max_charge = 0
        sum_running = 0
        for j in range(i, n):                                              # extend the window one robot at a time
            max_charge = max(max_charge, charge_times[j])
            sum_running += running_costs[j]
            k = j - i + 1
            cost = max_charge + k * sum_running
            if cost <= budget:
                best = max(best, k)
            else:
                break                                                       # further extension only makes k (and thus cost) larger
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(maximum_robots([3, 6, 1, 3, 4], [2, 1, 3, 4, 5], 25))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking the running max and sum incrementally avoids rescanning the whole window at every extension step.

Breaking out once the cost exceeds budget is a valid pruning, since the cost formula only ever grows (both the max charge time and k*sum can only increase or stay the same) as the window extends further.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly finds the largest valid consecutive group, since every possible starting point is directly checked, extending until the budget is exceeded.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^2) does not scale to the problem's constraints (up to 5*10^4 robots); a sliding window combining a monotonic deque and a running sum resolves the identical question in O(n).
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts tracking from scratch for every starting point. Instead, maintain a single sliding window (never restarting), tracked by a monotonic decreasing deque (for the current max charge time) and a running sum (for total running cost). As the window expands, update both; whenever the cost exceeds budget, shrink the window from the left, adjusting the running sum and popping the deque's front if needed.

Maintain a maxDeque (decreasing), a left pointer, and a running sumRunning. For each right index: update the deque (pop dominated back entries, push right), add runningCosts[right] to sumRunning. While the current window's cost (charge times[maxDeque.front] + k * sumRunning) exceeds budget: shrink left (subtract runningCosts[left] from sumRunning, pop the deque's front if it equals left), incrementing left. Update the best size as k = right - left + 1.
9. Optimized Solution
Maintain a sliding window tracked by a monotonic deque (for max charge time) and a running sum (for total running cost), shrinking from the left whenever the cost exceeds budget.
Dry run for chargeTimes = [11,12,19], runningCosts = [10,8,7], budget = 19

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Every single-robot window already exceeds the budget, so the maximum valid group size is 0, matching the expected result.

codes.python:
from collections import deque

def maximum_robots(charge_times, running_costs, budget):
    max_deque = deque()                                                    # DECREASING deque of indices: front is always the window's max charge time
    left = 0
    sum_running = 0
    best = 0
    for right in range(len(charge_times)):
        while max_deque and charge_times[max_deque[-1]] <= charge_times[right]:
            max_deque.pop()                                                # maintain decreasing order
        max_deque.append(right)
        sum_running += running_costs[right]

        k = right - left + 1
        while max_deque and charge_times[max_deque[0]] + k * sum_running > budget:
            if max_deque[0] == left:
                max_deque.popleft()                                        # the window's current max leaves as we shrink
            sum_running -= running_costs[left]
            left += 1
            k = right - left + 1

        best = max(best, k)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(maximum_robots([3, 6, 1, 3, 4], [2, 1, 3, 4, 5], 25))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): each index is pushed onto the deque exactly once and popped at most once (from either end) across the entire algorithm.
Space: O(n), for the deque in the worst case.
Why This Works

The monotonic decreasing deque always exposes the window's current maximum charge time at its front, exactly as in the standard sliding window maximum technique. The running sum stays perfectly synchronized with the window's total running cost, since it is updated by exactly the amount the window's membership changes by. Checking the combined cost formula directly against these two efficiently-maintained values (no rescanning) correctly determines validity at every step, and shrinking exactly when needed maintains the invariant that the window is always as large as currently possible.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The deque stores INDICES (not charge times), so checking "does the window's left boundary now exclude the deque's front" during shrinking is a simple index comparison.
The running sum (sumRunning) is adjusted by simple addition (on expansion) and subtraction (on shrinking), never recomputed from scratch.
Using a wide integer type (long/long long) for the cost calculation is essential, since k * sumRunning can grow very large given the problem's constraints.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (restart tracking for every start index)","O(n^2)","O(1) extra","Correct, but repeats overlapping work across different starting points"],["Optimized (sliding window, monotonic deque + running sum)","O(n)","O(n)","Maintains both the window's max charge time and running cost sum incrementally"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a sliding window's validity depends on a COMBINATION of aggregates (here, a max AND a sum), each aggregate can be tracked with its own appropriate technique (a monotonic deque for the max, a running total for the sum) simultaneously, all updated incrementally as the window both grows and shrinks.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting that the cost formula multiplies the running cost SUM by k (the current window size), not just adding a flat sum, which changes as the window's size itself changes.
Using a 32-bit integer type for the cost calculation, risking overflow given how large k * sumRunning can become.
Forgetting to update the monotonic deque's FRONT during shrinking, leaving a stale (out-of-window) index that would give an incorrect max charge time.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly identifying that the cost formula needs BOTH a max (monotonic deque) and a sum (running total) tracked simultaneously demonstrates recognizing this as a combination of two familiar sliding-window sub-techniques.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "A sliding window's cost/validity depends on BOTH a max and a sum" points toward combining a monotonic deque (for the max) with a simple running total (for the sum), maintained together.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this build on Sliding Window Maximum? It reuses the EXACT SAME monotonic deque technique for tracking the window's max, here combined with an additional running sum for the second part of the cost formula.

Why is it safe to always shrink from the LEFT (never needing to reconsider a different shrinking strategy)? Because the window represents a CONTIGUOUS group, and once its cost exceeds budget, removing the LEFTMOST element is the only way to shrink it while keeping it contiguous; there is no alternative removal strategy to consider.

How would you adapt this if MULTIPLE different cost formulas needed to be checked simultaneously? Each additional aggregate (max, min, sum, etc.) needing efficient window-tracking would require its own appropriate technique (deque for extremes, running total for sums), all maintained in parallel exactly as done here.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct combination of the monotonic deque technique from Sliding Window Maximum with a simple running-sum sliding window, both foundational techniques reused throughout this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (sliding window, monotonic deque + running sum): O(n) time, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sliding window combining a monotonic deque (for max) with a running sum

Core Idea: Track the window's max charge time via a monotonic decreasing deque, and its total running cost via a simple running sum; shrink from the left whenever the combined cost (max + k*sum) exceeds budget
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: The window's cost depends on TWO different aggregates (a max and a sum), each requiring its own appropriate incremental-tracking technique, maintained together
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Monotonic deque for max charge; running sum for running costs; while max+k*sum>budget, shrink left
